title: Dormancy gate — is the rose in the window for structural pruning?

common.applies_to: Established bush rose. Prerequisite for structural and whole-bush pruning (PKR-OBS/DEC-000002, 000005, 000006, and any shortening or shaping of healthy canes). Does not govern removal of wood confirmed dead, damaged or diseased (PKR-DEC-000001, PKR-DEC-000004), which follows the removal-only session.
common.preserved_uncertainty: AF-3 (Moderate): in mild or warm-winter climates, full leaf loss may not occur and premature bud break is a documented risk — the gardener should judge dormancy by bud state specifically, not by whether leaves are present. A follow-up commission (FRD-BUSHROSE-DORMANCY-02, submitted alongside this package) is testing whether the bud-swell signal itself needs a stated mild-climate exception; this gate's wording will be revised if that research changes the picture.

content.question: Look closely at the buds along your rose's canes. Are they still tight and closed, or just beginning to swell? Or have leaves opened and new shoots started to grow?
content.caveat: In a mild winter, a rose may keep some of its leaves, so judge by the buds, not by whether the leaves have dropped. Warm spells can also start buds growing early.

answers.dormant: Still dormant — buds are tight and closed, or just beginning to swell; no new leaves have opened anywhere
answers.growing: Active new growth is already well underway — leaves have opened and new shoots are clearly growing

content.notSureFallback: That's alright — have another look at the buds, not the leaves: are they still tight and closed, or have any started to swell or open?

intro.text: Your rose is already growing, so full pruning now is likely to reduce or delay flowering. One source says pruning is fine until there is a couple of inches of new growth. You can still remove wood that is dead, damaged or diseased.

removalOnly.notSureIntro: Since I can't be sure your rose is still dormant, I'll leave full pruning for now. You can still remove wood that is dead, damaged or diseased.

conditions.text: Remove only the wood you are sure is dead, damaged or diseased. Heavy pruning of healthy canes at this stage can reduce flowering.
Go gently and avoid damaging the new leaves.
Cut back to healthy wood, where the inside of the cane (the pith) is white.
For anything that looks like canker (sunken, discoloured patches on a cane) or other disease, cut well below the affected part, and bin the prunings or burn them where local rules allow.

lateSeason.text: Pruning late in the growing season is discouraged, because it can encourage new growth that winter cold may damage. Diseased wood can still be cut out, including in the autumn, and dead and damaged wood can be removed at any time.
